summary: Sharply eroded buttes and pinnacles banded in tan, red and yellow, set in the largest undisturbed mixed-grass prairie in the United States. The rock holds one of the world's richest beds of mammal fossils; bison, bighorn sheep and black-footed ferrets live on the grass above it.
story: The Badlands are layers of sediment — the floor of an ancient inland sea, then the mud, ash and sand of rivers and floodplains — laid down between about 75 and 28 million years ago and now being taken apart. The White River and its creeks cut into the soft rock quickly, around an inch a year in places, carving the buttes, spires and gullies of the Badlands Wall.

That erosion keeps uncovering fossils. The rocks are among the richest anywhere for the mammals of the Oligocene: early horses, rhinoceroses, sabre-toothed cats and the sheep-sized oreodonts. Visitors have made some of the important finds — the Pig Dig began in 1993 when two hikers noticed bones weathering out of a hillside.

Above the rock lies the largest undisturbed mixed-grass prairie in the United States, protected in the Badlands Wilderness. Bison were returned to it in the 1960s and black-footed ferrets, once thought extinct, in the 1990s; prairie dog towns, bighorn sheep and pronghorn share the grass.

The Lakota called this land mako sica, bad land. The park's South Unit lies within the Pine Ridge Reservation and is managed with the Oglala Lakota; one of the last Ghost Dances took place on Stronghold Table in 1890, weeks before the massacre at Wounded Knee, 45 miles south. The area became a national monument in 1939 and a national park in 1978.

sights.name: Notch Trail
sights.note: A canyon walk and a log ladder up to a notch with a view over the White River valley.

sights.name: Door Trail
sights.note: A short boardwalk through a break in the Badlands Wall into a maze of eroded formations.

sights.name: Fossil Exhibit Trail
sights.note: A boardwalk with casts of the fossils found in the park, beside the formations they came from.

sights.name: Yellow Mounds Overlook
sights.note: Rounded hills of bright yellow and red fossil soils, the oldest exposed layers in the park.

sights.name: Pinnacles Overlook
sights.note: A wide view south over spires and gullies to the prairie, often with bighorn sheep nearby.

sights.name: Roberts Prairie Dog Town
sights.note: A busy prairie dog colony on the Sage Creek Rim Road.

sights.name: Sage Creek Basin Overlook
sights.note: A view over the wilderness prairie where the park's bison range.

sights.name: Big Badlands Overlook
sights.note: The first view of the Badlands Wall from the Northeast Entrance, and a sunrise favourite.

entrances: Pinnacles Entrance, from Interstate 90 exit 110 near Wall
Interior Entrance, on SD 377 from the town of Interior
lodging: Cedar Pass Lodge, inside the park near the Ben Reifel Visitor Center
seasonalClosures: Summer brings heat and sudden thunderstorms with hail and lightning; winters are cold, with snow

chronology.text: One of the last Ghost Dances is held on Stronghold Table, before the massacre at Wounded Knee.
Part of the South Unit becomes an aerial gunnery range.
Badlands is redesignated a national park.
Two visitors discover the fossil site known as the Pig Dig.

safety: Prairie rattlesnakes live here. Watch where you put your hands and feet, especially off trail.
Thunderstorms build fast in summer. Get off exposed ridges and out of washes when one approaches.
Give bison a wide berth — at least 25 yards — and never approach them.
regulations: Fossils may not be collected. Leave a find where it lies and report it at a visitor center.
Drones may not be launched, landed or flown in the park.
